1. We don't need whitelist configuration mechanism for session channels, as session channels already provide a mechanism to control the same using user privilege and privilege of the commands.
Let me know if you find any reason why this whitelist configuration must exist for session based channel.

2. For session-less channels, currently we want to have this filtering mechanism to host interface alone, as other we assume it is trusted. So, question here is why we need this restriction on that interface?

Basically, trying to understand why it is require? or in which scenario we are trying to address here?
In some cases, vendors need to mask access to certain commands for certain channels, just as commands does not exist, not just the user privilege, and the whitelisting mechanism works well.

Can you please elaborate the case here (trying to understand the scenarios here, which will not be covered by the existing 2 cases).
1. We have user based privilege restriction
2. We have channel based privilege restriction
i.e. we will be able to tell on channel 1 (say eth0), execute only operator privilege commands only even though the user is admin privilege user.

Trying to understand the redefinition of these whitelist commands filtering here, which can't be covered in existing one (which is again not specification complaint here).

A case is when the BMC manages storage devices, the vendor needs to mask some commands that even the administrator can't execute, and this case cannot be controlled with user privilege or channel privilege. This situation is similar to the firmware firewall in the specification. However, the most similar firmware firewall in OpenBMC is the whitelist filtering mechanism. Due to actual needs, the static whitelist mechanism is currently implemented.

I think the bash fu has gotten complicated enough that it's useful to give an example of how the line would look _without_ placeholders:

# Turn "0x00:0x00 // Chassis:Get Chassis Capabilities" -> "{ 0x00, 0x00, 0x0000 }, // Chassis:Get Chassis Capabilities"

Hmm. I don't know how many people are fluent in awk. It's probably OK to put a comment over this line saying something like:

# Count how many instances of 0x exist by splitting on '0x' and counting the number of fields created, then reducing the count by one.

That means that "0xab:0xcd // foobar" must split into "", "ab:", and "cd // foobar" (NF=3).

I don't think this is very obvious. "number of separators = (number of separated areas) - 1" is already not very obvious, and the fact that awk will make an empty field in front of a separator given with -F is also not obvious.

I think there are some other ways you could do this:

1)
You could trim the comment and then count the number of fields you see when you split on ':':
echo $line | grep -Po "0x..(:0x[0-9a-f]+)+" | awk -F ':' '{print NF}'
or
echo $line | grep -Po ".*(?=//)" | awk -F ':' '{print NF}'

This approach is nice because the awk part is obvious, but the regular expression is not obvious - especially if you use the one with backreferences.

2)
You could ask grep to print the matched sections (one per newline) and count them, to more explicitly count '0x' sections:
echo $line | grep -o 0x | wc -l

This approach is nice because the regex is very obvious and it avoids use of awk. However, the method is a little confusing (print each 0x match to a new line, then count the number of lines produced).

Since you're piping anyways, I'd say that approach #2 is most concise for what you're really doing (counting the number of hex fields provided in the line).

Given the complexities of parsing the config lines into code, it might be a good idea to use python instead of a giant pipeline of bash-executed text editing executables. It would be more readable and easier to maintain.

Do we know that the command will always be a 16b hex, like in the above case (0x0000)?

I'd prefer to see the regex more restrictive, i.e. "0x[a-f0-9]{4}".  Especially because, for me, six '.' strung together is kind of hard to read :) I have to get my face really close to the monitor and count to see how many characters we expect...

This line wants a comment; it takes a lot of thinking to understand what you're doing here.

I guess you're getting the number of entries in the whitelist which don't have a channel set, and then comparing it to the total size of the whitelist; if you have entries in the whitelist that don't have a channel set, then you need to process channel restrictions.

There are a few problems:

- Why are you casting whitelist.size() to an int? I think you'd be able to compare size_t to a count_if output (although I'm having trouble telling from the docs what that type would end up being)....?
- You shouldn't be doing a C-style cast ( "(int)foo" or "int(foo)" ) anyways.
- Why are you implicitly casting the channel value to a bool? That's confusing to follow too.
- The logic seems inverted; you're comparing "total list size" to "total list size where a condition isn't true".  This is a little convoluted and difficult to follow...

Ultimately you're trying to say:

"bool channelsRestriction = (are there entries in the whitelist which have a channel besides 0x0000?)"

You could just use find_if() for this, right? Something like the following:

```
// If any whitelist members specify a channel, we need to check channel restrictions.
channelsRestriction = std::find_if(whitelist.cbegin(), whitelist.cend(), [](const netfncmd_tuple& first) { return std::get<2>(first) != 0x0000; });
```

It's probably tempting to leave it at "return std::get<2>(first)" but I think the implicit cast to bool is a little confusing, when you're really looking for "no channel set". Better yet, if there is a constant somewhere which names 0x0000 as "no channel" then you should compare to that.

Hmm, isn't this logic duplicated, except that in the "channelsRestriction == false" case it's assumed that channel # is 0x0000?

Why don't you combine the logic and do a check at the time that you're building the tuple instead?

With all the lambdas and <algorithms> methods flying around it's a little confusing to read, so I suggest you create some helpers to make this method a little more functional and readable, and try to combine the two cases here. Otherwise, I think we will run into trouble trying to fix both of them when our handling requirements change.
